key_terms.meaning: States of a p-body MOS capacitor: holes at the surface (V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub>); holes pushed away (V<sub>G</sub> > V<sub>FB</sub>); electron layer when φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub>.
Cutoff V<sub>GS</sub> < V<sub>T</sub>; linear V<sub>GS</sub> ≥ V<sub>T</sub> and V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>; saturation V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.

V<sub>T0</sub> = V<sub>FB</sub> + 2φ<sub>F</sub> + √(2qε<sub>si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>)/C<sub>ox</sub>, with V<sub>FB</sub> = φ<sub>MS</sub> − Q<sub>ox</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub> and φ<sub>F</sub> = (kT/q) ln(N<sub>A</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>).

Linear: I<sub>D</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)[V<sub>ov</sub>V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2]; saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>², with k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> and V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.
µ<sub>eff</sub> = µ<sub>0</sub>/(1 + θV<sub>ov</sub>): the vertical field lowers mobility.
v = µE/(1 + E/E<sub>c</sub>), E<sub>c</sub> = v<sub>sat</sub>/µ; for short L, I<sub>Dsat</sub> → WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>V<sub>ov</sub>, linear in overdrive.
Saturation: C<sub>gs</sub> ≈ ⅔C<sub>ox</sub>WL + C<sub>ov</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub> = C<sub>ov</sub>; linear: ½C<sub>ox</sub>WL + C<sub>ov</sub> each; C<sub>ov</sub> = C<sub>ox</sub>WL<sub>ov</sub>.
C<sub>j</sub> = C<sub>j0</sub>/(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ<sub>B</sub>)<sup>m</sup>, bottom (per area) plus sidewall (per perimeter).
L, W, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>T</sub> ÷ S and N<sub>A</sub> × S: delay 1/S, power per gate 1/S², power density 1.
P = αC<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>²f; power-delay product PDP = P<sub>avg</sub>·t<sub>p</sub>, the energy per switching event.
Drain-induced barrier lowering: V<sub>T</sub> falls as V<sub>DS</sub> rises, in mV/V.
SS = 2.3nφt, at least about 60 mV/decade at 300 K; I<sub>off</sub> = I<sub>VT</sub>·10<sup>−V<sub>T</sub>/SS</sup>.
W<sub>eff</sub> = 2H<sub>fin</sub> + W<sub>fin</sub> per fin (tri-gate), in whole fins.

takeaways: A MOS capacitor becomes a transistor once the gate inverts the surface and the source and drain connect to the inversion layer.
Accumulation, depletion and inversion describe the surface charge; cutoff, linear and saturation describe the shape of the channel.
The threshold voltage is a budget of flat band, band bending and depletion charge; reverse body bias adds to it.
The square law gives the long-channel current from V<sub>ov</sub>, W/L and k<sub>n</sub>′; its ½ and its region test are the most-tested details.
Mobility degradation, velocity saturation and channel length modulation make short devices weaker than the square law and give the output curve its slope.
Every terminal pair is a capacitor whose share depends on the region; series resistances slow the charging.
Constant-field scaling keeps power density constant; constant voltage raises it as S³, which is why V<sub>DD</sub> had to fall until leakage stopped it.
Below threshold the current falls only one decade per 60 to 100 mV, so leakage sets standby power, and FinFETs regain gate control to keep it low.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the MOS capacitor states with the region tests, the threshold voltage with body effect, the square-law equations with their derivation, the non-ideal effects, the device capacitances, and scaling with its power and short-channel effects. Draw the cross-section or the characteristic each time.

bank.q: Explain the accumulation, depletion and inversion states of a MOS capacitor on a p-type body. Sketch the charge in each state and the C-V curve, and say what each state means for the transistor.
outline: Structure: gate, oxide of thickness t<sub>ox</sub>, p body; C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub>
Accumulation for V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub>: holes at the surface, C = C<sub>ox</sub>
Depletion for V<sub>G</sub> > V<sub>FB</sub>: ionised acceptors, width W<sub>d</sub>, C<sub>dep</sub> in series, C falls
Inversion at φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub>: electron layer; C back to C<sub>ox</sub> at low frequency, stays low at high frequency
Meaning for the transistor: cutoff below V<sub>T</sub>, channel above V<sub>T</sub>; threshold defined at strong inversion
answer: Structure. A metal or polysilicon gate sits on silicon dioxide of thickness t<sub>ox</sub> over a p-type body with acceptor doping N<sub>A</sub>. Gate, oxide and body form a parallel-plate capacitor with C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub> per unit area. The flat-band voltage V<sub>FB</sub> is the gate voltage at which the surface holds no net charge; the three states are measured from it.

Accumulation (V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub>). The gate carries negative charge. It attracts holes, the majority carriers, into a thin sheet right at the oxide. The charge pair is negative on the gate and positive holes at the surface, separated only by the oxide, so the capacitance per unit area is C<sub>ox</sub>.

Depletion (V<sub>G</sub> a little above V<sub>FB</sub>). The gate is positive and repels holes from the surface, leaving the fixed negative acceptor ions in a depletion layer of width W<sub>d</sub>. The surface potential φ<sub>s</sub> (the band bending) rises with V<sub>G</sub>. The depletion layer behaves as a second capacitor C<sub>dep</sub> = ε<sub>si</sub>/W<sub>d</sub> in series with the oxide, so C = C<sub>ox</sub>C<sub>dep</sub>/(C<sub>ox</sub> + C<sub>dep</sub>) is less than C<sub>ox</sub>, and it falls as W<sub>d</sub> grows.

Inversion (φ<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2φ<sub>F</sub>). The positive gate also draws electrons, the minority carriers, to the surface. When φ<sub>s</sub> reaches 2φ<sub>F</sub>, where φ<sub>F</sub> = (kT/q) ln(N<sub>A</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>), the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density: the surface is n-type. The depletion width stops growing (at its maximum W<sub>dmax</sub>), and further gate charge is balanced by more electrons in the thin inversion layer. The gate voltage at which this happens is the threshold voltage V<sub>T</sub>.

answer.text: C-V curve. At low frequency the inversion electrons follow the signal and sit at the oxide, so C returns to C<sub>ox</sub>; at high frequency they cannot be generated fast enough and C stays at the minimum set by W<sub>dmax</sub>.

answer: Meaning for the transistor. Add n⁺ source and drain regions. In accumulation and depletion there is no electron path between them, so the nMOS is in cutoff. In inversion the electron layer connects source and drain: this is the channel, and its charge per unit area is about C<sub>ox</sub>(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>). The transistor regions (linear and saturation) are then decided by how V<sub>DS</sub> shapes that channel.

Check with numbers: for N<sub>A</sub> = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ at 300 K, φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.026 ln(10¹⁷/1.5 × 10¹⁰) = 0.41 V, so inversion needs a band bending of 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.82 V, and the maximum depletion width is √(2ε<sub>si</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>/(qN<sub>A</sub>)) = √(2 × 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.817 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10²³)) = 0.10 µm.

bank.q: Derive the threshold voltage of an nMOS transistor in terms of the flat-band voltage, the surface potential and the depletion charge, and extend it to include the body effect. Explain each term.
outline: Flat band: V<sub>FB</sub> = φ<sub>MS</sub> − Q<sub>ox</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub>
Strong inversion at φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub>
Depletion charge Q<sub>dep</sub> = √(2qε<sub>si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>); oxide voltage Q<sub>dep</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub>
V<sub>T0</sub> = V<sub>FB</sub> + 2φ<sub>F</sub> + Q<sub>dep</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub>; threshold-adjust implant qDI/C<sub>ox</sub>
With V<sub>SB</sub>: surface must reach 2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub>; V<sub>T</sub> = V<sub>T0</sub> + γ[√(2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub>) − √(2φ<sub>F</sub>)]
answer: Set-up. An nMOS on a p body with doping N<sub>A</sub>, oxide capacitance C<sub>ox</sub> per unit area, source and body at the same potential. Threshold is the gate-to-source voltage at which the surface reaches strong inversion, φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub>. The gate voltage divides into a voltage across the oxide and the surface potential, after the flat-band offset is removed.

Term 1, flat band. The gate and the body have different work functions (difference φ<sub>MS</sub>), and the oxide holds fixed positive charge Q<sub>ox</sub> per unit area. The gate voltage that cancels both and makes the bands flat is V<sub>FB</sub> = φ<sub>MS</sub> − Q<sub>ox</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub>.

Term 2, band bending. Strong inversion needs the surface potential to rise by 2φ<sub>F</sub>, where φ<sub>F</sub> = (kT/q) ln(N<sub>A</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>): φ<sub>F</sub> brings the surface to intrinsic, and a second φ<sub>F</sub> makes it as n-type as the body is p-type.

Term 3, depletion charge. At φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub> the depletion width is W<sub>d</sub> = √(2ε<sub>si</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>/(qN<sub>A</sub>)), holding charge Q<sub>dep</sub> = qN<sub>A</sub>W<sub>d</sub> = √(2qε<sub>si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>) per unit area. This negative charge must be matched by positive charge on the gate, which needs a voltage Q<sub>dep</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub> across the oxide. At threshold the inversion charge is still zero, so nothing else is needed.

Threshold adjustment. A shallow implant of dose DI acceptors per unit area adds a sheet of negative charge at the surface, raising the threshold by ΔV<sub>T</sub> = qDI/C<sub>ox</sub>. Processes use it because the n⁺ poly gate alone gives a V<sub>T</sub> near zero.

Body effect. If the source is V<sub>SB</sub> above the body, the electrons in the channel come from the source, so the surface must reach φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub> before inversion. The depletion charge grows to √(2qε<sub>si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>(2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub>)), and the threshold rises by the difference of the two depletion terms:

answer: Check: each term has units of volts (γ in √V times √V), and V<sub>T</sub> rises with V<sub>SB</sub> but more slowly at larger V<sub>SB</sub>, as the square root predicts. For a pMOS all charges reverse sign and V<sub>Tp</sub> is negative.

bank.q: Derive the drain current of an nMOS in the linear and saturation regions using the gradual-channel approximation. State the condition for each region and sketch the output characteristics.
outline: Channel charge Q<sub>I</sub>(x) = C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)]
Drift: I<sub>D</sub> = WQ<sub>I</sub>(x)µ<sub>n</sub> dV/dx, constant along x
Integrate 0 to L: linear-region equation, valid for V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>ov</sub>
Pinch-off at V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> gives saturation I<sub>D</sub> = ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>²
Cutoff for V<sub>GS</sub> < V<sub>T</sub>; sketch of curves with the pinch-off parabola
answer: Assumptions (gradual channel): the field along the channel is much weaker than the field across the oxide, mobility µ<sub>n</sub> is constant, and the device is above threshold. Source at 0 V, x from 0 (source) to L (drain), channel potential V(x) from 0 to V<sub>DS</sub>.

Channel charge. The gate-to-channel voltage at x is V<sub>GS</sub> − V(x); the part above V<sub>T</sub> makes inversion charge: Q<sub>I</sub>(x) = C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)] per unit area.

Current. Electrons drift with velocity µ<sub>n</sub>·dV/dx. Current = width × charge per area × velocity: I<sub>D</sub> = W·µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)]·dV/dx. With no charge stored in steady state, I<sub>D</sub> is the same at every x.

answer.pre:
I<sub>D</sub> × (integral of dx from 0 to L) = Wµ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> × (integral of (V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V) dV from 0 to V<sub>DS</sub>)
I<sub>D</sub>·L = Wµ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>[(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2]
I<sub>D</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)[V<sub>ov</sub>·V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2],  k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>

answer: Linear region. The result holds while the charge is positive along the whole channel, which at the drain end means V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub> > V<sub>T</sub>, that is V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>ov</sub>. For small V<sub>DS</sub> the current is ≈ k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>·V<sub>DS</sub>: a resistor of value 1/[k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>].

Saturation. At V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> the drain-end charge is zero (pinch-off). Putting V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> into the bracket gives V<sub>ov</sub>² − V<sub>ov</sub>²/2 = V<sub>ov</sub>²/2, so I<sub>D</sub> = ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>². For larger V<sub>DS</sub> the extra voltage drops across the pinched-off gap and the ideal current stays at this value.
Cutoff. For V<sub>GS</sub> < V<sub>T</sub> there is no channel and I<sub>D</sub> ≈ 0 (only subthreshold leakage).

answer.text: Output characteristics with k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 2000 µA/V², V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V (the device of the I-V chapter):

answer: Sketch: each curve rises from the origin, bends over and goes flat at its knee; the knees lie on the dashed parabola I<sub>D</sub> = ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>DS</sub>², which divides the linear region (left) from saturation (right). The flat levels grow as V<sub>ov</sub>² (1 : 4 : 9 here).
Check: at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V, linear gives 2000 × (1.0 × 0.5 − 0.125) = 750 µA, below the 1000 µA saturation level, as it must be.

bank.q: List the capacitances of a MOSFET, explain where each comes from, and show how the gate capacitance divides between source, drain and body in each region.
outline: Oxide capacitance C<sub>ox</sub>WL
Overlap C<sub>ov</sub> = C<sub>ox</sub>WL<sub>ov</sub> per side (CGSO, CGDO)
Region table: cutoff, linear, saturation
Junction capacitances C<sub>sb</sub>, C<sub>db</sub>: area and sidewall, C<sub>j0</sub>/(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ<sub>B</sub>)<sup>m</sup>
Worked numbers; Miller effect on C<sub>gd</sub>
answer: The five capacitances are C<sub>gs</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub> and C<sub>gb</sub> (from the gate oxide and overlaps) and C<sub>sb</sub> and C<sub>db</sub> (from the source and drain junctions).
Oxide (intrinsic) capacitance. The gate and the channel or body form a plate capacitor through the oxide: C<sub>ox</sub>WL, with C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub>.

Overlap capacitance. Source and drain diffuse a distance L<sub>ov</sub> under the gate, so the gate overlaps each by C<sub>ov</sub> = C<sub>ox</sub>WL<sub>ov</sub>. SPICE gives it per unit width (CGSO, CGDO). It is present in every region, and fringing field is lumped with it.

answer: Junction capacitances. The n⁺ source and drain are reverse-biased junctions with the p body. Each has a bottom part (CJ per area) and a sidewall part (CJSW per perimeter), and both fall with reverse voltage: C<sub>j</sub> = C<sub>j0</sub>/(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ<sub>B</sub>)<sup>m</sup>, with m ≈ 0.5 for the bottom and 0.33 for the sidewall.

answer.text: Numbers (W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, t<sub>ox</sub> = 4 nm, L<sub>ov</sub> = 0.02 µm; drain 1 µm × 0.5 µm, CJ = 1 fF/µm², CJSW = 0.2 fF/µm, φ<sub>B</sub> = 0.9 V):

answer: Why it matters. These capacitances are what a driving gate charges and discharges, so they set delay and dynamic power. C<sub>gd</sub> is small, but the drain swings opposite to the gate in an inverter, so C<sub>gd</sub> sees about twice the voltage change (the Miller effect) and counts double in delay estimates.

Check: total gate capacitance in saturation 1.61 + 0.17 = 1.78 fF is less than the 2.16 + 0.35 = 2.50 fF the gate would present if all the area and both overlaps appeared at once, because the drain has lost its share of the channel.

bank.q: An nMOS has µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> = 200 µA/V², W/L = 10, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V and V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V. Find the region and I<sub>D</sub> for V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V and for V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V. Then find g<sub>m</sub>, the on-resistance near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, and the current at V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V if λ = 0.05 V⁻¹.
outline: k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 2000 µA/V², V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V
V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V < 1.0 V: linear, 510 µA
V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V ≥ 1.0 V: saturation, 1000 µA
g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mA/V; R<sub>on</sub> = 500 Ω
answer: Device constant: k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 200 µA/V² × 10 = 2000 µA/V². Overdrive V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 V, positive, so the transistor is not in cutoff.
Case 1, V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V. Region test: 0.3 V < V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V, so the channel is continuous: linear region.
Case 2, V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V. Region test: 2 V ≥ 1.0 V, so the drain end is pinched off: saturation.

answer.pre: I<sub>D</sub> = ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>² = ½ × 2000 µA/V² × (1.0 V)² = 1000 µA = 1.0 mA

answer: Transconductance (saturation): g<sub>m</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub> = 2000 µA/V² × 1.0 V = 2 mA/V. Check: g<sub>m</sub> = 2I<sub>D</sub>/V<sub>ov</sub> = 2 × 1.0 mA / 1.0 V = 2 mA/V.

On-resistance near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0: R<sub>on</sub> = 1/[k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>] = 1/(2000 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.0) = 500 Ω. Check against case 1: 0.3 V / 500 Ω = 600 µA, a little above the exact 510 µA because the V<sub>DS</sub>²/2 term already bends the curve at 0.3 V.
Channel length modulation in saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = 1000 µA × (1 + 0.05 × 2) = 1000 × 1.10 = 1.10 mA. The output resistance is r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>) ≈ 1/(0.05 × 1.0 × 10⁻³) = 20 kΩ.

Boundary between the regions: saturation begins at V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V, where both formulas give 1.0 mA. Below 1.0 V the current climbs along the linear branch; above it the ideal current stays flat.

Power in the transistor at the saturated point: P = I<sub>D</sub> × V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 mA × 2 V = 2 mW (2.2 mW with λ). In the linear case it is only 510 µA × 0.3 V = 0.15 mW, which is why a switch that is fully on wastes little power.

Sensitivity to the gate: at V<sub>GS</sub> = 2.0 V the overdrive is 1.5 V. V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V is still linear, I<sub>D</sub> = 2000 × (1.5 × 0.3 − 0.045) = 810 µA; V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V is still saturation (2 ≥ 1.5), I<sub>D</sub> = ½ × 2000 × 1.5² = 2.25 mA. The saturated current grows as the square of the overdrive, the linear one only in proportion.
Check of continuity: at V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V the linear formula gives 2000 × (1.0 − 0.5) = 1000 µA, equal to the saturation value, so the two branches meet as they should.

bank.q: An nMOS with V<sub>T0</sub> = 0.4 V, γ = 0.4 √V and φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.35 V has its source 0.6 V above the body. Find the new threshold voltage and the fall in saturation current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.2 V. Explain why this matters in a NAND gate.
outline: V<sub>T</sub> = 0.521 V
Overdrive 0.8 V → 0.679 V
Current ratio (0.679/0.8)² = 0.72: 28 % less
Upper transistor of the NAND stack has V<sub>SB</sub> > 0
answer: Data: V<sub>T0</sub> = 0.4 V, γ = 0.4 √V, 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.70 V, V<sub>SB</sub> = 0.6 V, V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.2 V (measured from the source).
Overdrive. Without body effect V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.2 − 0.4 = 0.80 V. With it V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.2 − 0.521 = 0.679 V.

answer.text: Saturation current, I<sub>D</sub> ∝ V<sub>ov</sub>² with the same k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L):

answer: So the current falls by 28 % for the same gate voltage. If, say, k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 1 mA/V², the current drops from ½ × 1 × 0.64 = 0.320 mA to ½ × 1 × 0.461 = 0.230 mA.
Why. The reverse-biased source-body junction widens the depletion region, so more depletion charge must be supported before inversion; the gate needs 0.121 V more.

Recovering the current: to carry 0.320 mA again at the same gate voltage the transistor must be 1/0.720 = 1.39 times wider. Alternatively the gate voltage would have to rise by the same 0.121 V, to 1.321 V.

NAND gate. In a two-input NAND the two nMOS are in series between the output and ground. The lower one has its source at ground (V<sub>SB</sub> = 0). The upper one has its source at the middle node, which sits above ground while the output discharges, so it has V<sub>SB</sub> > 0, a higher V<sub>T</sub> and less current. The pull-down is therefore slower than two unbiased transistors would be, which is why the transistors of tall stacks are made wider and why stacks are limited to about four.
Check: the rise 0.121 V is less than γ√V<sub>SB</sub> = 0.4 × 0.775 = 0.31 V, as it must be, because the square root grows more slowly than linearly from 2φ<sub>F</sub>.

bank.q: A gate drives an inverter whose nMOS is 1 µm wide and pMOS 2 µm wide, both with L = 0.1 µm, C<sub>ox</sub> = 15 fF/µm² and overlap capacitance 0.2 fF/µm per side. The driver adds 0.8 fF of drain junction and the wire 1.0 fF. Estimate the load and the delay if the driver resistance is 5 kΩ.
outline: Gate capacitance of each transistor: C<sub>ox</sub>WL + 2C<sub>ov</sub>W
nMOS 1.9 fF, pMOS 3.8 fF
τ = RC = 37.5 ps; t<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.69RC = 26 ps
First-order RC model; delay scales with load and 1/W of driver
answer: Model. For a hand estimate take each input transistor's gate capacitance as its area term plus both overlaps, C<sub>ox</sub>WL + 2C<sub>ov</sub>·W (the worst case during switching, when the device passes through the linear region).
Total load on the driver: C<sub>L</sub> = 5.7 (fan-out) + 0.8 (own drain junction) + 1.0 (wire) = 7.5 fF.
The 0.69 factor is the time for an RC step response to reach half the supply, which is how propagation delay is defined.

Fan-out of four. If the gate drives four such inverters, C<sub>L</sub> = 4 × 5.7 + 0.8 + 1.0 = 24.6 fF, so τ = 5 kΩ × 24.6 fF = 123 ps and t<sub>p</sub> = 0.69 × 123 = 85 ps: more than three times slower.

Energy. Each charge-and-discharge cycle of the 7.5 fF load draws C<sub>L</sub>·V<sub>DD</sub>² from the supply; at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1 V that is 7.5 fJ per cycle, half stored and half lost in the driver resistance on the way up.

What changes the delay. Doubling the driver width halves R and halves the delay (if its own junction growth is small). Doubling the fan-out roughly doubles the 5.7 fF part, giving C<sub>L</sub> = 13.2 fF and τ = 66 ps. A shorter wire helps only its own 1.0 fF.

Limits. This is a first-order lumped RC model: the transistor resistance changes during the transition, C<sub>gd</sub> of the driver adds a Miller term, and the wire is distributed. Simulation or the Elmore and logical-effort methods refine it.
Check: units Ω × F = s; 5 kΩ × 7.5 fF = 37.5 × 10⁻¹² s. The fan-out is 76 % of the load, so sizing the next stage matters most.

bank.q: A 0.18 µm process (t<sub>ox</sub> = 4 nm, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V) has a gate with load 10 fF, drive current 1 mA and clock 500 MHz. Scale it by S = 2 with constant-field rules and tabulate the changes in V<sub>T</sub>, I<sub>D</sub>, C, delay, power per gate, area and power density. Compare with constant-voltage scaling.
outline: All lengths, V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>T</sub> ÷ 2; N<sub>A</sub> × 2
C 10 → 5 fF; I<sub>D</sub> 1 → 0.5 mA; delay CV/I 18 → 9 ps
Area ÷ 4, density constant, gates per area × 4
Constant voltage: P × 2, density × 8
answer: Constant-field rules with S = 2: divide L, W, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> by 2, multiply N<sub>A</sub> by 2. Every field (voltage/length) is unchanged.
Why I<sub>D</sub> falls as 1/S: I<sub>D</sub> = ½µC<sub>ox</sub>(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>²; C<sub>ox</sub> doubles, W/L is unchanged and V<sub>ov</sub>² falls by 4, so I<sub>D</sub> halves.

Field check: V<sub>DD</sub>/L = 1.8 V / 0.18 µm = 10 V/µm before and 0.9 V / 0.09 µm = 10 V/µm after, and the oxide field V<sub>DD</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub> = 0.45 V/nm in both, so reliability is unchanged. Doubling N<sub>A</sub> halves the depletion widths roughly in step with L, which keeps short-channel effects in check.
Why V<sub>T</sub> must scale too: if V<sub>T</sub> stayed at 0.5 V with V<sub>DD</sub> = 0.9 V, the overdrive would fall from 1.3 V to 0.4 V instead of 0.65 V and the speed gain would be lost.

Constant-voltage scaling (V<sub>DD</sub> stays 1.8 V, square-law device): I<sub>D</sub> = ½ × 2C<sub>ox</sub> × (W/L) × V<sub>ov</sub>² rises by S to 2 mA, delay = 5 fF × 1.8 V / 2 mA = 4.5 ps (÷ S²), clock 2 GHz, power = 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 3.24 × 2 × 10⁹ = 32.4 µW (× S), and power density rises × S³ = 8. Fields double, which threatens oxide breakdown and hot-carrier damage.

Conclusion: constant-field scaling gives 4 times the gates per mm², each 2 times faster and using 4 times less power, with the same heat per mm². Real processes stopped following it near V<sub>DD</sub> ≈ 1 V because V<sub>T</sub> could not fall further without leakage rising tenfold per 60 to 100 mV.

bank.q: A transistor has I<sub>off</sub> = 10 nA/µm at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 with V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 V and a subthreshold swing of 80 mV/decade at 300 K. Find the current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0.1 V, the static power of 20 mm of off width at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1 V, the effect of a 20 K temperature rise (SS ∝ T, V<sub>T</sub> falls 1.5 mV/K), and the V<sub>T</sub> increase that cuts leakage tenfold.
outline: I<sub>D</sub> = I<sub>off</sub>·10<sup>V<sub>GS</sub>/SS</sup>: 10 × 10<sup>1.25</sup> = 178 nA/µm
Leakage 10 nA/µm × 2 × 10⁴ µm = 200 µA, 200 µW
At 320 K: SS = 85.3 mV/dec, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.27 V; I<sub>off</sub> × 3.85
Tenfold cut: raise V<sub>T</sub> by one swing, 80 mV
Comment on standby budget
answer: Subthreshold law: on a log scale the current rises one decade per SS of gate voltage, so I<sub>D</sub>(V<sub>GS</sub>) = I<sub>off</sub> × 10<sup>V<sub>GS</sub>/SS</sup> below threshold, with I<sub>off</sub> the value at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0.
Static power of the block: total off width 20 mm = 2 × 10⁴ µm, so I<sub>leak</sub> = 10 nA/µm × 2 × 10⁴ µm = 2 × 10⁵ nA = 200 µA, and P = V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>leak</sub> = 1 V × 200 µA = 200 µW.

So a 20 K rise multiplies the leakage by about 3.9 (taking the current at threshold as fixed): the block now leaks about 770 µA, 0.77 mW. Both effects push the same way, and hot chips leak more, which heats them further.

Energy over a day of standby: 200 µW × 86 400 s = 17.3 J at 300 K, but 0.77 mW × 86 400 s = 66.5 J at 320 K. For a battery-powered device the temperature of the chip in a pocket matters as much as the transistor choice.

Sketch: on a log-current axis the subthreshold curve is a straight line through 10 nA/µm at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 and 178 nA/µm at 0.1 V, rising one decade per 80 mV up to threshold at 0.3 V; heating makes the line less steep and moves it left.

Tenfold reduction: one decade of current needs one swing of gate voltage, so raising V<sub>T</sub> by SS = 80 mV cuts I<sub>off</sub> from 10 to 1 nA/µm and the block power from 200 µW to 20 µW. The cost is a smaller overdrive and a slower gate, which is why high-V<sub>T</sub> cells are used only off the critical paths.
Check: 10<sup>80/80</sup> = 10, and 178 nA at 0.1 V is still far below the current at threshold, 10 × 10<sup>0.3/0.08</sup> nA = 56 µA, so the subthreshold law applies at 0.1 V.

bank.q: Explain how velocity saturation and channel length modulation each change the square-law model. For a 50 nm nMOS (W = 1 µm, µ<sub>n</sub> = 300 cm²/V·s, v<sub>sat</sub> = 10⁷ cm/s, C<sub>ox</sub> = 0.02 F/m², λ = 0.5 V⁻¹) at V<sub>ov</sub> = 0.6 V, compare the square-law and velocity-saturated currents and find the intrinsic gain. Which effect dominates?
outline: Square-law assumptions
Velocity saturation: v = µE/(1 + E/E<sub>c</sub>), V<sub>DSsat</sub> and I<sub>Dsat</sub> formulas, linear-in-V<sub>ov</sub> limit
Numbers: E<sub>c</sub> = 3.33 × 10⁶ V/m, E<sub>c</sub>L = 0.167 V, V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 0.31 V, I<sub>Dsat</sub> = 0.58 mA vs 2.16 mA
CLM: r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>) = 3.5 kΩ; g<sub>m</sub> = 1.30 mS; gain ≈ 4.5
Velocity saturation sets the current; CLM and DIBL set the gain
answer: Square-law assumptions: constant mobility, carrier velocity proportional to field, a channel that ends exactly at the pinch-off point. Short channels break the second and third.

Velocity saturation. With v = µE/(1 + E/E<sub>c</sub>) and E<sub>c</sub> = v<sub>sat</sub>/µ, the linear-region current is divided by (1 + V<sub>DS</sub>/(E<sub>c</sub>L)). The current peaks, and the device saturates, at V<sub>DSsat</sub> = E<sub>c</sub>L[√(1 + 2V<sub>ov</sub>/(E<sub>c</sub>L)) − 1], with I<sub>Dsat</sub> = WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>(V<sub>ov</sub> − V<sub>DSsat</sub>). For E<sub>c</sub>L ≫ V<sub>ov</sub> this returns to the square law; for E<sub>c</sub>L ≪ V<sub>ov</sub> it tends to WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>V<sub>ov</sub>, linear in overdrive and independent of L.

Channel length modulation. Past saturation the depleted gap at the drain grows with V<sub>DS</sub>, the effective length becomes L − ΔL and the current rises: I<sub>D</sub> ≈ I<sub>Dsat</sub>(1 + λV<sub>DS</sub>), giving a finite output resistance r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>).

answer.text: Numbers for the 50 nm device (SI units: µ<sub>n</sub> = 0.03 m²/V·s, v<sub>sat</sub> = 10⁵ m/s, W/L = 20):

answer: So the square law over-predicts the current 3.7 times: velocity saturation decides the drive current of this device.

answer.pre:
g<sub>m</sub> = WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>[1 − 1/√(1 + 2V<sub>ov</sub>/(E<sub>c</sub>L))] = 2 × 10⁻³ × (1 − 1/2.864) = 1.30 mS
   (square law would give k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub> = 0.012 × 0.6 = 7.2 mS)
r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>) = 1/(0.5 × 0.579 × 10⁻³) = 3.45 kΩ
g<sub>m</sub>·r<sub>o</sub> = 1.30 × 10⁻³ × 3.45 × 10³ ≈ 4.5

answer: An intrinsic gain of about 4.5 is far below the 20 to 50 of long-channel devices: CLM (together with DIBL, which also lowers V<sub>T</sub> as V<sub>DS</sub> rises) sets the output resistance and so the gain.

Which dominates? For drive current and delay, velocity saturation (3.7× less current, g<sub>m</sub> 5.5× below the square law). For analog gain, CLM and DIBL. A digital designer worries about the first, an analog designer about the second; both make the square law unusable at 50 nm without corrections.

Design response: analog stages use longer L than the minimum (λ falls roughly as 1/L, so r<sub>o</sub> rises), while digital gates use minimum L and accept the linear-in-V<sub>ov</sub> current, often fitted by the alpha-power law with α ≈ 1.2 to 1.5.
Check: V<sub>DSsat</sub> 0.311 V < V<sub>ov</sub> 0.6 V, as velocity saturation requires, and I<sub>Dsat</sub> < square-law value; the gain 4.5 > 1, so the device still amplifies.

bank.q: A short-channel nMOS (the device of the non-ideal effects chapter: 0.86 mA at V<sub>ov</sub> = 2 V, g<sub>m</sub> = 0.573 mA/V, λ = 0.1 V⁻¹, DIBL 100 mV/V) shows less current than the square law at high V<sub>GS</sub> and a rising slope in saturation. Explain both observations quantitatively, and discuss hot-carrier damage, LDD and NBTI.
outline: Low current: mobility degradation and velocity saturation (3.44 mA predicted, 0.86 mA)
Slope: CLM gives λI<sub>D</sub> = 0.086 mA/V; DIBL gives g<sub>m</sub> × η = 0.057 mA/V; total 0.143 mA/V, r<sub>o</sub> ≈ 7 kΩ
Hot carriers near the drain; LDD lowers the peak field at a resistance cost
NBTI raises |V<sub>T</sub>| of pMOS over time
Effect on timing margins and design
answer: Observation 1, low current. The square law predicts ½k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>² = ½ × 1.72 mA/V² × 4 = 3.44 mA. Two effects lower it. Mobility degradation (vertical field) divides by (1 + θV<sub>ov</sub>). Velocity saturation (lateral field) caps the carrier speed: with E<sub>c</sub>L = 0.5 V, V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 0.5(√9 − 1) = 1.0 V and I<sub>Dsat</sub> = WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>(V<sub>ov</sub> − V<sub>DSsat</sub>) = 0.86 mA, four times less. At high V<sub>GS</sub> the current grows roughly linearly with V<sub>ov</sub>, not as its square.
Observation 2, rising slope. Two mechanisms raise I<sub>D</sub> with V<sub>DS</sub> in saturation.

answer.text: Their contributions to the slope of I<sub>D</sub> against V<sub>DS</sub>:

head: Mechanism
Cause
Slope
rows: pinch-off point moves towards the source; I<sub>D</sub> ≈ I<sub>Dsat</sub>(1 + λV<sub>DS</sub>)
V<sub>T</sub> falls by η = 0.1 V per volt of V<sub>DS</sub>; the current rises by g<sub>m</sub> × ΔV<sub>T</sub>

answer: Without DIBL the output resistance would be 1/(0.086 mA/V) = 11.6 kΩ; DIBL lowers it by 40 %. The two can be told apart: DIBL also shifts the subthreshold curves sideways with V<sub>DS</sub>, CLM does not.

Hot carriers. The lateral field peaks at the drain end. Electrons there gain enough energy to be injected into the oxide or to break silicon-hydrogen bonds at the interface. The trapped charge and interface traps raise V<sub>T</sub> and lower mobility over months to years, so drive current falls with age, worst at high V<sub>DD</sub>.

LDD. A lightly doped n⁻ extension between the channel and the n⁺ drain spreads the drain voltage over a longer distance, lowering the peak field and the hot-carrier rate. The price is series resistance (tens of ohms per µm of width), which lowers I<sub>D</sub> and g<sub>m</sub> slightly. It is accepted because a device that degrades over its lifetime is worse than one that is a few percent slower.

NBTI. A pMOS held with its gate low (negative V<sub>GS</sub>) at high temperature slowly builds interface traps and positive oxide charge, so |V<sub>Tp</sub>| rises by tens of millivolts over years and the pull-up slows. It partly recovers when the stress is removed, which makes it depend on the workload. Its nMOS counterpart in high-k processes is PBTI.

Evaluation for design. Timing is signed off with aged models (end-of-life V<sub>T</sub>), adding margin of a few percent to every path; the supply is limited by oxide and hot-carrier reliability; analog circuits use longer channels to reduce both CLM and DIBL.
Check: the slopes add to 0.143 mA/V; over a 1 V rise in V<sub>DS</sub> the current increases from 0.86 to about 1.0 mA, a visible but modest slope, as measured curves show.

bank.q: Compare a planar bulk nMOS with a FinFET for gate control, leakage, drive width, threshold setting and variability. Use SS = 90 mV/decade (planar) and 65 mV/decade (FinFET) at the same V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 V, and a fin of W<sub>fin</sub> = 10 nm, H<sub>fin</sub> = 30 nm.
outline: Planar: gate on one side; FinFET: three sides of a thin, fully depleted fin
I<sub>off</sub> ratio 10<sup>−0.3/0.065</sup> / 10<sup>−0.3/0.09</sup> = 0.052: about 19× less leakage
Same I<sub>off</sub> allows V<sub>T</sub> = 0.217 V and more overdrive
W<sub>eff</sub> = 70 nm per fin; quantised widths
V<sub>T</sub> by work function; less dopant variation; costs: 3D parasitics, process
answer: Gate control. In a planar device the gate covers only the top of the channel; in a short channel the drain field reaches the source end through the body underneath (DIBL, roll-off). In a FinFET the gate covers the top and both sides of a fin thinner than its depletion width, so the body is fully depleted and the drain field lines end on the gate. The FinFET keeps the source barrier under gate control.

answer.text: Leakage at the same V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 V (I<sub>off</sub> ∝ 10<sup>−V<sub>T</sub>/SS</sup>):

answer: So the FinFET leaks about 19 times less at the same threshold, assuming equal current at threshold. Alternatively, for the same I<sub>off</sub> the FinFET may use V<sub>T</sub> = 0.3 × 65/90 = 0.217 V, giving 83 mV more overdrive and more on-current at the same V<sub>DD</sub>.

Drive width. A planar width is drawn freely. A tri-gate fin has W<sub>eff</sub> = 2H<sub>fin</sub> + W<sub>fin</sub> = 2 × 30 + 10 = 70 nm, and widths come in whole fins: 700 nm needs 10 fins, 720 nm needs 11 (770 nm). Tall fins give more width per unit of chip area.

Current per footprint: at 1 mA per µm of effective width, one fin carries 70 µA. Ten fins at a fin pitch of, say, 30 nm occupy 300 nm of layout width but give 700 nm of channel width, more than twice what a planar device of the same footprint would give.

Threshold setting and variability. Planar V<sub>T</sub> is set by body doping and implants, and the random number of dopant atoms in a tiny channel makes V<sub>T</sub> vary from device to device. The FinFET body is undoped, so V<sub>T</sub> is set by the gate work function; random dopant variation largely disappears, though fin width variation adds its own spread.

Judgement: below about 22 nm the FinFET is the better device for logic, because leakage and variability, not raw current, limit planar scaling. Its costs (fin patterning, higher gate-to-contact capacitance, quantised widths) are accepted. Gate-all-around nanosheets extend the same idea to four sides.
Check: 10<sup>1.28</sup> = 19.1, and 0.217 V / 0.3 V = 65/90, as the swings require.

bank.q: Explain why leakage became a first-order concern in scaled CMOS, and evaluate the design knobs for reducing it. Use a chip with 5 × 10⁷ µm of off width at I<sub>off</sub> = 1 nA/µm, V<sub>DD</sub> = 0.9 V, and an active switched capacitance αC = 0.5 nF at 1 GHz.
outline: Scaling lowered V<sub>DD</sub> and so V<sub>T</sub>; I<sub>off</sub> grows tenfold per SS
Numbers: leakage 50 mA, 45 mW; dynamic 0.405 W; standby power is all leakage
Other paths: gate tunnelling, GIDL, junctions
Knobs: high-V<sub>T</sub> cells, power gating, body bias, stacking, temperature; each with numbers
Trade-off with speed
answer: Why leakage grew. Constant-field scaling lowers V<sub>DD</sub>, and V<sub>T</sub> must fall with it to keep the overdrive. But the subthreshold current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 is I<sub>off</sub> ∝ 10<sup>−V<sub>T</sub>/SS</sup>, and SS cannot go below about 60 mV/decade at room temperature. Every 60 to 100 mV taken off V<sub>T</sub> multiplies the leakage of every off transistor by ten. With billions of transistors and V<sub>DD</sub> near 1 V, the sum became comparable with switching power. Thin oxides add gate tunnelling, and sharp drain fields add GIDL.
In a phone in standby, the clocks stop and dynamic power is near zero, so leakage alone drains the battery: 45 mW for a whole day is about 1.1 Wh.

answer.text: Knobs, applied to the same chip:

head: Knob
How it works
Effect here
Cost
rows: High-V<sub>T</sub> cells (+80 mV, SS = 80 mV/dec) on 80 % of the width
one decade less current per swing
slower cells, only off critical paths
Power gating of 90 % of blocks in standby
a header or footer switch cuts the supply
wake-up time, switch area, state loss
raises V<sub>T</sub> through the body effect
the middle node rises, giving negative V<sub>GS</sub> and body effect
only where the logic has stacks
SS ∝ T and V<sub>T</sub> falls with T
a 60 K rise can multiply leakage about 36 times

answer: Evaluation. Multi-V<sub>T</sub> libraries and power gating give the largest cuts in practice and are used in every mobile chip; body bias is effective in planar and FD-SOI processes but weaker in FinFETs; thermal control matters because leakage and temperature feed each other.
Trade-off. Each knob that raises the effective V<sub>T</sub> lowers speed or adds latency, so designers spend low-V<sub>T</sub>, fast cells only on the critical paths and gate off what is idle.
Check: 0.5 nF × 0.81 V² × 1 GHz = 0.405 W; 12.6 mW is 3.6 times below 45 mW; power gating then leaves 10 % of 12.6 mW = 1.26 mW.

glossary.def: State of a MOS capacitor with majority carriers drawn to the surface, below flat band for a p-type body.
Rise of V<sub>T</sub> when the source is reverse biased with respect to the body; set by the coefficient γ.
Shortening of the effective channel as V<sub>DS</sub> rises in saturation, which makes I<sub>D</sub> rise with V<sub>DS</sub>.
Logic that pairs an nMOS pull-down network with a complementary pMOS pull-up network, so no static current flows in steady state.
Region with V<sub>GS</sub> < V<sub>T</sub>: no channel, only leakage.
State of a MOS capacitor with majority carriers pushed away, leaving fixed dopant ions.
Drain-induced barrier lowering: V<sub>T</sub> falls as V<sub>DS</sub> rises in short channels.
Gate voltage at which the silicon surface holds no net charge: V<sub>FB</sub> = φ<sub>MS</sub> − Q<sub>ox</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub>.
Transistor whose channel is a thin vertical fin with the gate on its top and sides.
Gate-induced drain leakage: band-to-band tunnelling in the drain under the gate overlap when the gate is low and the drain high.
Carriers given high energy by the drain field that damage the oxide or interface and shift V<sub>T</sub> over time.
State in which minority carriers form a surface layer of the opposite type; strong inversion at φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub>.
Lightly doped drain: an extension that lowers the peak drain field at the cost of series resistance.
Region with a continuous channel, V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>; also called triode or ohmic.
Fall of carrier mobility as the vertical gate field rises.
Negative bias temperature instability: slow rise of |V<sub>T</sub>| in a pMOS held with its gate low at high temperature.
V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>, the gate voltage above threshold that makes channel charge.
Capacitance where the gate overlaps the source or drain: C<sub>ov</sub> = C<sub>ox</sub>WL<sub>ov</sub>.
Vanishing of the channel charge at the drain end when V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.
Average power times propagation delay; the energy per switching event.
Region with the channel pinched off at the drain, V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.
Gate voltage per decade of subthreshold current, SS = 2.3nφt.
Gate-to-source voltage at which the surface reaches strong inversion.
g<sub>m</sub> = ∂I<sub>D</sub>/∂V<sub>GS</sub>, the change of drain current per volt of gate voltage.
Levelling of carrier drift velocity at about 10⁷ cm/s at high lateral field.
